claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by a dynamically re-forming, self-healing passivating oxide layer.
Synergistic interactions among multiple principal elements promote formation of the self-healing oxide layer.
The proposed initial alloy has a polished, uniform, single-phase microstructure, exemplified by an FCC phase.
The proposed initial alloy retains an unaltered native oxide layer.
Simultaneous mechanical wear and exposure to an acidic chloride solution locally remove the surface oxide.
Selective elemental segregation at the surface produces a fine-grained, multilayer oxide film.
The fine-grained, multilayer oxide film acts as a barrier against mechanical abrasion.
The fine-grained, multilayer oxide film acts as a barrier against corrosive attack.
The multicomponent alloy composition enables rapid reformation of the protective oxide after local wear removal.
Rapid oxide reformation minimizes exposure of the underlying metal.
Minimizing exposure of the underlying metal reduces wear-induced damage and corrosive degradation.
The proposed self-healing alloy will have lower cumulative mass loss than a mechanically matched alloy with suppressed oxide-reformation ability.
The proposed self-healing alloy will have lower pit loss than the matched baseline.
Intermittent intact oxide regions within wear scars will indicate in-situ oxide repair.
The prediction should hold when oxide-reformation kinetics can counteract oxide-removal kinetics under moderate wear and corrosive conditions.
The prediction may fail at sufficiently high wear rates because oxide regeneration cannot keep pace with removal.
The prediction may fail in non-oxidizing media or at extreme pH where effective oxide regeneration does not occur.
Direct evidence for the proposed mechanism under simultaneous mechanical and corrosive loading is limited.
